title: India's Gen Z Cockroach Movement Plans Massive March to Parliament as Wangchuk Forcibly Removed
excerpt: Tens of thousands expected to march to India's Parliament on Monday after police stormed the protest site and hospitalized hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk.
body:
• Tens of thousands of protesters plan to march to India's Parliament on Monday, the first day of its Monsoon Session, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over exam paper leaks.
  • Police forcibly removed hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk from the Jantar Mantar protest site on Saturday after 20 days without food, sparking outrage.
  • CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has escalated demands to include Prime Minister Modi's resignation and taken over the hunger strike from Wangchuk.
  • Bollywood actor Hrithik Roshan broke the industry's silence by publicly supporting Wangchuk, resharing his video on Instagram and writing "this sounds true."

A Movement Born From a Joke

What started as a sarcastic social media quip has grown into India's largest youth-led protest movement in years. The Cockroach Janta Party, a satirical "people's party" founded by former Boston University student Abhijeet Dipke, is preparing to lead a mass march to Parliament on Monday — the opening day of the Monsoon Session — in what could become the defining confrontation between India's Gen Z and the Modi government.

The movement's name comes from India's Chief Justice, who casually likened unemployed youth and government critics to "cockroaches" and "parasites." Dipke's response on X — "What if all cockroaches came together?" — went viral. Within days, millions had signed up on his website, and his Instagram amassed millions of followers.

Wangchuk's Forced Removal Inflames the Movement

On Saturday morning, plainclothes police officers entered the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi, stormed the stage, covered it with white curtains, and whisked away Sonam Wangchuk — the 59-year-old Ladakhi engineer and educator who had been on a hunger strike since June 28. Police cited a court order and Wangchuk's "deteriorating health condition," but his wife Gitanjali J Angmo accused the government of "illegal detention disguised as medical care."

Wangchuk had lost approximately 20 percent of his body weight over 20 days without food. In a video released late Friday, he said he intended to stay alive for the July 20 march, adding that if people failed to show up, he would "return as a ghost."

"I learnt about the trauma students go through when I played a teacher in one of my movies," referencing his role as educator Anand Kumar in the 2019 film Super 30."

"They dragged Sonam Sir away while hurling abuse at him. A 60-year-old man, who had been on a hunger strike for 20 days and hadn't eaten a thing, was forcibly dragged away by the Delhi Police."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP founder

Images of the operation went viral, drawing thousands more to Jantar Mantar by Saturday evening. Dipke, who had been assaulted twice in the past month — slapped at an event in Jaipur and attacked with blue ink-like substance on Saturday — broke down and pledged to continue the hunger strike himself.

What the Protesters Want

The CJP's core demands center on India's broken examination system. Back-to-back scandals involving NEET paper leaks, technical glitches, and cancelled tests have triggered outrage across the country. Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms to competitive examinations, compensation for families of students who died by suicide over the leaks, and the resignation of Education Minister Pradhan.

After Wangchuk's forced removal, Dipke escalated: "Until now, we were demanding Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation, but after this despicable act, we will now demand the resignation of Narendra Modi."

Three doctoral students — Neha Bora, Aameen Amitoj, and Manish — from the All India Students Association had joined Wangchuk on his hunger strike before his removal.

Bollywood Breaks Its Silence

In a notable departure from Bollywood's typical silence on political controversies, actor Hrithik Roshan publicly backed Wangchuk by resharing a video posted by actress Lisa Ray on his Instagram Stories. In the video, Wangchuk questions why so many people have remained silent about the examination irregularities and highlights that 20 students have taken their own lives.

Roshan wrote: "This sounds true. I learnt about the trauma students go through when I played a teacher in one of my movies," referencing his role as educator Anand Kumar in the 2019 film Super 30. His post marked one of the first instances of a mainstream Bollywood superstar expressing solidarity with the movement.

Why the Diaspora Is Watching

South Asia has become ground zero for Gen Z protest movements, with Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Nepal all seeing mass protests topple governments in recent years. India has the world's largest Gen Z cohort, facing unemployment, record inequality, and what democracy watchdogs describe as democratic backsliding since 2014.

For the Indian diaspora, the movement raises uncomfortable parallels. Many NRIs left India partly because of the competitive examination system's pressures. The spectacle of young Indians demanding accountability from a government that has not held a press conference in over 12 years resonates deeply with those who experienced the system's worst excesses firsthand.

What Happens Monday

New Delhi is on high alert. Heavy police and paramilitary deployments have been ordered around Parliament and the surrounding areas. Multiple activist groups and opposition political parties have expressed solidarity with the march and urged people to join. Wangchuk's wife has petitioned the court to transfer him from a government hospital to a private facility. CJP spokesman Saurav Das told Al Jazeera: "This march is to reclaim our India. It is the fight for a better future, not just for students but for this country as well."
